effect: certain proteins turn glassy inside cells and let them survive drying out
how: A drought does not usually kill a crop slowly: a hot dry fortnight at flowering wipes out the year's yield even though rain comes later. Tardigrades survive complete drying because certain proteins turn the inside of their cells to glass, holding every structure in place until water returns. A cereal given those genes, switched on only when the leaf dries out, could pause instead of dying and resume when the rain arrives.
obstacle: Glassy cells cannot photosynthesise, so the plant must judge when to shut down and when to wake, and getting it wrong costs the harvest anyway.
why: The proteins work in yeast and human cells; a whole crop pausing and restarting is untested.
real: Tardigrade CAHS/TDP genes raise desiccation tolerance in yeast, bacteria and cultured cells and a patent claims transgenic drought-tolerant plants, but the only plant work found is a 2025 Arabidopsis/agroinfiltration manuscript with inconsistent expression and no field or whole-crop pause-and-resume demonstration.
